04Freelance

Designing a livestream censor, then designing it again

LiveGuard watches a stream as it goes out and mutes what would get the streamer demonetized. I joined as the only designer, drew the product the client asked for — and then spent the rest of the project taking it apart as the team found out what five developers could actually build.

Role
UI/UX design, prototyping, branding
Timeline
August 2023 → ongoing
Team
Me, solo designer · 5 devs
Tools
Figma, FigJam
Prototype
Open in Figma→

01 — The problem

One slip in a six-hour stream can cost you the whole day.

Demonetization is a platform pulling your ability to earn from something you made — for a policy breach, or just for content advertisers don’t want to sit beside. The rules tighten every year, YouTube’s most of all.

A creator can stream for six hours and lose the recording to a few seconds they don’t remember saying. The usual fix is to catch it in the edit afterwards, which means watching your own stream end to end before anyone else can.

LiveGuard’s bet was that the fix belongs earlier: censor it live, as it goes out, so there is nothing to clean up and nothing to appeal.

02 — The solution

A web app that sits beside the stream, not in front of it.

Streamers already have a setup that works — a broadcast tool, a platform, a routine they don’t want touched five minutes before going live. So LiveGuard had to be a companion to that setup rather than something you stream through.

Three words had to mean one thing to everybody before I could draw a single screen. Most of the first month’s confusion turned out to be this, not the interface:

  • Action — a segment of audio or video the user wants caught.
  • Event — an Action together with its Reaction: what gets caught, and what happens to it when it is.
  • Streaming profile — a set of Events switched on together. This one didn’t survive; see below.

03 — First pass

Everything the client asked for, drawn once.

There was no competitor to tear down. Nobody had shipped real-time censorship for livestreams, so the usual move — find the three apps closest to this and learn from their mistakes — wasn’t available. Requirements got refined in meetings instead, with the team members who actually stream.

What the client proposed

  • An in-stream controls overlay
  • A dashboard: event sets, an analytics preview, quick search
  • A streaming profiles page
  • A triggers library, with custom triggers
  • An events library, with custom events
  • An analytics page

What users needed

  • Controls simple enough to flip mid-stream
  • Visibility into what actually got censored
  • An obvious path for connecting the external app
  • A clean, monochrome interface that doesn’t compete with the stream

Who it’s for

  • Christie, 24 Twitch + YouTube · part-time creator
    About

    Christie makes vlogs and streams on more than one platform, then edits the recordings down herself before they go up on YouTube. The stream is the fun part; the edit is the job.

    Pain points
    • Hours of editing per stream
    • Can’t police her own vocabulary for six hours straight

04 — The cut

Then the scope met the calendar.

Three things landed at once, and between them they took out most of what I had just finished drawing.

  1. Time

    The release phases were fixed, and the requirements weren’t going to fit inside them. Something had to come out.

  2. Resources

    Five developers, and most of their attention was on the machine learning — which is the product. Interface work was what was left over.

  3. Complexity

    With no market example to point at, a first-time user has nothing to pattern-match against. The more we kept, the more there was to explain.

05 — Second pass

Card sorting, and a much smaller product.

I card-sorted the feature set with the team rather than defending it, which made the argument about what a user needs first instead of about what we’d already built. Three things changed:

  • Custom actions and events came out. The pre-set list covers swear-word censoring, and nothing else — for now.
  • Streaming profiles became platform grouping. Users already think in platforms; the profile was an abstraction on top of one they had.
  • Quick search came out. With this much less in the product, there wasn’t enough left to search.

06 — User testing

Three things testing caught that I hadn’t.

Moderated sessions with people who actually stream. Every one of these is something I was confident about going in.

  1. One overlay per platform, not one overall

    I’d designed a general in-stream overlay. Streamers don’t work generally — key binds and placement are per platform, and a shared overlay fights the setup they already have.

  2. The calendar took too many clicks

    Scheduling a stream was several steps longer than anyone expected it to be. Cut down and re-ordered.

  3. Stream keys belong on the dashboard

    Everyone went to the dashboard to edit theirs. It wasn’t there — it was in settings, where I’d filed it because that’s where settings go.

And then one more cut

Late on, technical constraints took two more things off the board. Analytics went entirely — it was a whole page, and it was the least load-bearing one. The in-stream overlay went with it as priorities moved, and with it every customization option that had existed to serve it.

07 — Design system

Blue, because blue already reads as protection.

The product is a guard. Blue is what people already associate with being looked after — it’s the colour of the people you call — so it didn’t need explaining. Dark mode came straight from the users: streamers work in the dark and their tools do too.

One sans-serif, no second face. The interface has to disappear behind a stream that isn’t about it.

The component library is still partway. Everything drawn is consistent, but it isn’t finished — which makes it the top of my list, because handoff to five developers is the thing it exists to make cheap.

08 — Where it landed

Still open, and the scope is finally honest.

This was my first freelance project taken end to end, and what shaped it most wasn’t a design decision — it was limited resources and guidelines that weren’t clear until we were already building against them. Some of the first iteration may come back once the team has room. None of it is promised.

What I’d do next

  1. More user tests

    The three that came back from the first round were the useful part of the whole project. There should have been more of them, earlier.

  2. Edge cases

    Everything drawn so far assumes the stream goes as planned. Most of them don’t.

  3. Finish the design system

    Partial is worse than none when five people are building from it.

What I took away

  1. Scope is a design decision, and it comes first

    I drew the whole product before anyone had said out loud what five developers could build in the time. That conversation was cheap and I had it late.

  2. Ask what the team can’t do

    Capability came up as a limit only when we hit it. Asking about it directly, early, would have saved a full iteration.

  3. Vocabulary before interface

    Action, Event, Profile — the month where those three meant slightly different things to different people cost more than any screen did.

  4. Cutting is not losing

    The second prototype is a better product than the first, and it is roughly half the size. That was not obvious to me at the time.
